extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, psychoanalysis, and humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and classifying jokes according to Freud's psychoanalytic framework (techniques, purposes, and effects), with attention to verbal vs conceptual forms and innocent vs tendentious aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification (making of an unsuspected connection)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke technique founded on unification — making an unsuspected connection or addition to a previous analogy so that the prolongation or extension produces a comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud emphasizes that prolonging an analogy or adding to it (a 'making of an addition to a previous analogy') can itself create a joke. Example: continuing a childlike comparison of new books to illnesses and then extending the analogy to represent their subsequent fate. Unification is treated as a distinct technical source of humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by absurdity / bewildering juxtaposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke arises from a striking juxtaposition or combination that sounds absurd or bewildering, so that the comic impression is due to the bewildering character of the juxtaposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lichtenberg examples (e.g., 'bread-bread fame') are cited: the surprise of a strange combination yields the joke. Freud calls this method 'representation by absurdity' and treats it as a familiar joking technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of remarkable epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: Using an unexpected or bewildering epithet (adjective) attached to a noun produces comic effect; the epithet becomes the vehicle of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'learned entrails', 'moral backside', 'breeches of respectability'. The odd adjective-noun pairing evokes amazement and laughter; sometimes the epithet alone carries most of the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debasing juxtaposition (abstract with low/concrete)
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtaposing something of a high or abstract category with something concrete, commonplace, or low (a 'debasement') often contributes to the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud notes many analogies are 'to a great degree

rubrics_metrics.name: Everyday-domain analogies (role-bound incongruity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour often arises when abstract notions are expressed via analogies drawn from the speaker's everyday occupations or mundane domain, producing incongruity between content and domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a clerk using analogies from his business life ('showcase of the imagination ... stocked with goods from the past'); the joke depends partly on the fact that such abstractions are brought into connection with ordinary things of the speaker's life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation and formation of a substitute (core of verbal jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal jokes often rely on condensation (bringing elements together) accompanied by formation of a substitute; these processes are central technical operations producing humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud treats condensation and substitute-formation as the core of the technique of verbal jokes, and links them to the dream-work mechanisms; they help produce the compressions and double-meanings that make word-based jokes effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement
rubrics_metrics.description: A conceptual joke technique where emphasis or meaning is shifted from its ordinary place, producing puzzling or comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Displacement contributes to the puzzling appearance of jokes (and dreams); it is listed alongside other conceptual techniques such as faulty reasoning and absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faulty reasoning / nonsensical representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using illogical, nonsensical, or obviously 'stupid' reasoning as a deliberate device to produce humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include apparent stupidity that masks deeper insight (e.g., 'cats have two holes cut in their skin precisely at the place where their eyes are'). Freud notes that what appears as stupidity can sometimes point to substantive problems (teleology, evolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect representation / allusion / symbolism akin to analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing a thought by an allusion, small symbol, or remote hint so the hearer reconstructs the intended meaning; indirect representation is a common joke technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud equates indirect representation with analogy-like symbolism; it distinguishes the mode of expression of dreams and is used in jokes (especially refined smut) to suggest forbidden content without explicit statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by the opposite
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressing something via its opposite as a comic device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud notes representation by the opposite is common in dreams and jokes and even accounted for in popular dream-interpretation; it's one of several conceptual joke techniques (with displacement, absurdity, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of sound / play upon words (verbal techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploiting similarity of sound, puns, and wordplay to create comic effect; typical of verbal jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a joke based on misreading ('Agamemnon' vs 'angenommen'), Schüttelreime (shaking-up rhymes), and 'experience consists in experiencing...' — Freud discusses how apt wordplay can deceive listeners into overvaluing the substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stupidity (feigned ignorance) as technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraying stupidity or naïveté to produce a comic effect; apparent stupidity can hide insightful commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud gives examples where 'stupidity' plus other techniques (e.g., similarity of sound) yields humour; he also stresses that such 'stupidity' can mask real theoretical problems (e.g., teleology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal vs conceptual classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify jokes by the material handled: 'verbal' jokes operate on sounds/words, 'conceptual' jokes operate on thoughts/concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud insists this is an independent classification from purpose (innocent/tendentious): both verbal and conceptual jokes can be innocent or tendentious; examples and techniques differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innocent (abstract) vs tendentious classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify jokes by purpose: 'innocent' (abstract) jokes are ends in themselves and non-tendentious; 'tendentious' jokes serve a purpose (hostility or exposure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud prefers 'innocent' to 'abstract' and stresses that innocent jokes are not necessarily trivial; the classification is independent of verbal/conceptual form and affects audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendentious purposes: hostile (aggressiveness/satire/defence) or obscene (exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a joke is tendentious it serves one of two purposes: hostility (aggressiveness, satire, defence) or obscenity (exposure) — these subsume the non-innocent aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud emphasizes that the same technical methods can be used for both purposes; tendentious jokes, by virtue of their aim, may access sources of pleasure unavailable to innocent jokes and thus often provoke stronger laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure derives from joke technique (not only content); reduction removes laugh
rubrics_metrics.description: The enjoyable effect of a joke is largely produced by its technical form; when a joke is 'reduced' (form replaced while preserving sense), it loses its comic power even if the thought remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud argues that technique (condensation, displacement, indirect representation) evokes pleasure in the hearer; examples (e.g., 'home-roulard') show pleasure cannot always be attributed to intellectual content or purpose alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined impression: substance vs joking envelope (misattribution risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our enjoyment of a joke is a combined impression of its substantive thought and its effectiveness as a joke, and we may be misled into overvaluing one component over the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud warns that apt thought-content can trick us into calling a sentence a brilliant joke, or vice versa; only upon 'reduction' do we realize which element carried the impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic value: prefer innocent/trivial jokes for theory
rubrics_metrics.description: For theoretical analysis of joke mechanisms, innocent (non-tendentious) and trivial jokes are more valuable because they present the problem in a 'purer' form without purpose-driven confounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud selects very simple, non-tendentious verbal jokes (e.g., Schüttelreime, home-roulard) as ideal material for isolating technical methods that produce pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-person structure of tendentious jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendentious jokes commonly involve three persons: the joker (speaker), the object-target of aggressiveness or sexual exposure, and a third person (listener) in whom the joke's pleasurable aim is fulfilled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud describes dynamics: the joker's aggression or sexual impulse is inhibited by the target and redirected toward or shared with the listener; the listener, not the joker, usually experiences the enjoyment. This structure explains why tendentious jokes can be socially effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smut/exposure as a tendentious (obscene) joke form
rubrics_metrics.description: Smut (obscene speech) functions as exposing the sexual object; it aims to make the assailed person imagine the sexual act and show that the speaker is imagining it, often serving seduction or hostile exhibitionism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud details smut's psychological basis: rooted in childhood exhibitionism and libido for looking/touching; smut historically directed at women, becomes a joke when addressed to a listener or when refined through allusion. Conditions favoring smut-jokes include the woman's resistance and the presence of a third person; refinement uses allusion and other joke methods to allow smut to be tolerated in 'good society.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical refinement of smut: allusion and reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: In refined social contexts, obscene material must be presented indirectly (allusion), so the hearer reconstructs the obscene content in imagination; greater discrepancy between form and implied content yields more refined humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud explains that the more remote the hint relative to the implied obscenity, the more socially acceptable and 'refined' the joke becomes; smut that attains the characteristics of a joke can also employ all standard verbal and conceptual techniques.
